summary:
Bourgogne-Franche-Comté stands under the French national framework. Rules on identity documents, anti-discrimination, criminal law, marriage and gender recognition are set by national statute and apply uniformly across metropolitan and overseas regions, so the legal rules a visitor faces in this region are the same ones that apply elsewhere in France.

Detention carries the sharpest documented risk. France has no statutory rule governing where a trans prisoner is held: placement follows the gender inscribed on identity documents, and each facility improvises, using special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describes trans women incarcerated on that basis as falling into a legal grey area, punished beyond their alleged crimes, with accounts of heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

The CGLPL, France's national custodial-inspection authority, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations of fundamental rights across all places of detention: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty. The recommendations also extend to intersex and non-binary detainees, and the national preventive mechanism told the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the earlier one produced no marked improvement and because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, which argued that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of questioning by French border police at the airport, conducted in front of other travellers.

In everyday movement, accommodation and services, France's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition. The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights confirming fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony, citing the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and setting out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition the baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
The region's own documented restriction concerns public assembly, and it fell on an event with a long local history. The prefecture banned the Pride 2025 march from central Dijon on 12 June 2025, citing "risk of trouble to public order"; it was the second consecutive year of the same restriction, and the only prefecture in France found to have twice banned a Pride march from its city centre with the ban upheld. The organisers' withdrawal citing LGBT visibility was itself called significant by the city.

On 14 June 2025 the administrative court rejected the legal challenge, and the march, about 1,500 people per police estimates, proceeded on a diverted route around the historic centre. Pride marches have been organised since 2013 in Chalon-sur-Saône, Dijon and Auxerre, so the Dijon gathering was an established regional event with over a decade of local history rather than a first-time gathering.

Nationally, pride marches have grown since the mid-1990s, spreading to provincial cities from 1994-1995 onward. Wikipedia's national 'LGBTI en France' page, the framework document every French region stands under, records legal protections against discrimination while stating that LGBT people continue to be the target of discrimination and violence, with reports of such incidents rising. Against that baseline the Dijon restriction is an exception rather than the rule.
localsOnly:
Detained trans people in France can refer their treatment to the CGLPL, which has received roughly 40 such referrals since 2010 and whose opinion of 25 May 2021 carries binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty. The national preventive mechanism has said its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

Complaints about discrimination in services go to the Défenseur des droits, whose framework decision on trans rights confirms persistent fundamental-rights violations and supplies official guidance that service providers are expected to follow.

Gender recognition is governed by the 2016 legal reform, and marriage has been open to same-sex couples since the law of 17 May 2013. Placement of trans prisoners has no statutory rule and is decided facility by facility, which leaves residents with no legal entitlement to a particular placement.

Parliamentary channels remain available: oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly put a trans woman's incarceration directly to the Keeper of the Seals, and placement conditions remain under parliamentary scrutiny.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records trans-specific violence, police conduct, or detention conditions at establishments within Bourgogne-Franche-Comté itself. The prison findings are national in scope, and none of them is tied to a named facility in this region.

Whether the CGLPL's binding guidance of 25 May 2021 has been implemented at any place of deprivation of liberty in the region is not sourced here.

The date of the Défenseur des droits framework decision is not stated in the inventory, and the outcome of any further appeal against the 14 June 2025 administrative court ruling on the Dijon march is unresolved.

Screening practice for trans travellers at French entry points rests on a single first-person account from 2017; whether document checks at airports follow any written procedure, and how they are conducted now, are not sourced.

Whether the 64% discrimination figure reported in the 2023 EU Fundamental Rights Agency survey breaks down for Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, and whether national anti-discrimination protections have been enforced in the region, are not addressed in the inventory.
